summary: Describes how a device can send location-related measurements to a Location Information Server in a request, helping it improve accuracy. It defines basic measurements including network attachment and assisted GNSS.

eli5.summary: You tell the map helper clues about where you are, and it works out better.

questions: what is a location information server
how does a device send wifi measurements to a lis
subtitle: How a device can hand its own network and radio observations to a location server so the server can place it more accurately.

tldr.problem: A Location Information Server (LIS) works out a device's location from what it knows about the network, but the device can see things the LIS cannot see, or can only get at higher cost.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an XML measurements container that rides inside a location request such as a HELD request, plus measurement types for LLDP, DHCP relay agent information, WiFi, cellular, GNSS and DSL, and a measurementRequest element the LIS can use to ask for more.
tldr.outcome: The LIS can use or ignore the data. Measurements are treated as privacy sensitive as location itself and can be falsified, so the RFC sets rules on protection, retention and validation, and adds a source label to PIDF-LO.

facts.label: Measurement types
facts.value: LLDP, DHCP relay agent info, WiFi, cellular, GNSS, DSL

facts.label: Transport protection
facts.value: TLS MUST be used over HELD

today: RFC 7105 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2014. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Devices Report Measurements
sections.content:
A Location Configuration Protocol (LCP) lets a Device ask its access network where it is. A Location Information Server (LIS) answers, using what it knows about the network and the physical environment. The LIS can get measurements from network elements, but a Device can often observe things about its own network attachment or surroundings that the LIS cannot get, or can only get at a higher cost in time or some other metric.

Giving the LIS this data gives it more options. Better accuracy is one gain; faster responses and lower error rates are others. The RFC defines how a Device reports location-related measurement data, with examples based on HELD (RFC 5985). Examples of such data are radio signal strength or timing, Ethernet switch identifiers and port identifiers. The data does not necessarily hold location directly, but can be combined with context or algorithms to derive it.
sections.eli5: The helper that knows where you are sometimes cannot see what you see. If you tell it, it can answer faster and more exactly.

sections.title: The Measurements Container
sections.content:
The core is an XML measurements element that can be added to a location request in any protocol that carries XML, such as a HELD request. It holds one or more measurement elements. The LIS can ignore measurement data it does not support or understand. Changes that could break compatibility MUST be added as new measurement definitions, not as extensions to existing types.

Common attributes on the container:

  • time: when the measurement was made, which can differ from when it was reported. It SHOULD be provided whenever possible.
  • expires: how long the data is expected to be valid, and also a way for the Device to ask the LIS not to keep it longer. A Device that does not want data retained can omit it.
  • timeError: an upper bound on the RMS time error in seconds.

Individual measurements can carry rmsError (root-mean-squared error, in the same units as the measurement) and samples (how many samples went into the value). Measurements with different types, or that need independent times, cannot share a container and need multiple measurement sets.
sections.eli5: The container is a labelled envelope for your clues. It says when you saw them, how long they stay true, and how sure you are.

sections.title: Requests and Source Labels
sections.content:
The LIS can ask for data. A measurementRequest element names the measurement types wanted through a measurement element whose type is an XML qualified name, optionally with a samples count. In HELD, including one in an error response with code locationUnknown signals that providing measurements would make a later request more likely to succeed. In other HELD messages it has undefined semantics and can be ignored.

The LIS can use or ignore measurements, as long as the privacy rules are respected. The RFC also extends the Presence Information Data Format - Location Object (PIDF-LO, RFC 4119) with a source element naming the type of measurement source:

  • lis: data the LIS or sources it trusts acquired. It MAY be used if Device data was completely validated.
  • device: the LIS MUST include this if the location is based in whole or part on Device data that is not completely validated.
  • other: data from a third party. The LIS MUST include it unless it trusts that third party.

A combination of tags MAY be given. The RFC also says the PIDF-LO method SHOULD be adjusted to reflect the method used.
sections.eli5: The helper can say, "I cannot tell yet, show me what signals you see." And every answer is stamped to say whether the helper or you supplied the clues.

sections.title: The Measurement Types
sections.content:
Each type lives in its own XML namespace, and new parameters must be added in a new namespace rather than to an existing one.

  • LLDP: identifies the adjacent node (chassis) and its port, as hexadecimal values reported exactly as received. Repeat the lldp element for multiple neighbours.
  • DHCP relay agent information: opaque circuit, remote and subscriber identifiers, plus giaddr. Any of the three identifiers MAY be omitted if unknown. The subscriber value MUST NOT go to a LIS not authorized to receive information about the access network.
  • 802.11 WiFi: one or more access points (ap), where only bssid is mandatory. Optional items include ssid, channel, flightTime and signal data such as rcpi and rsni.
  • Cellular: serving and observed cells for LTE, UMTS, GSM and CDMA, using global identifiers such as MCC and MNC for 3GPP networks.
  • GNSS: per-satellite doppler, codephase and cn0 values, with system and signal attributes. It is taken from the first stage of satellite receiving, so a LIS can combine it with other data if too few satellites were seen.
  • DSL: data a LIS operated by an ISP can pass to the infrastructure provider's LIS, such as an L2TP tunnel, a RADIUS access node with slot and port, Ethernet VLAN tags (S-TAG and C-TAG), or an ATM virtual circuit (VPI and VCI).

Cellular, WiFi and GNSS types also have request forms so a LIS can ask for specific kinds or parameters.
sections.eli5: Different clues suit different places: the name of the nearest network box, the Wi-Fi hotspots you can hear, the nearby phone towers, or signals from satellites.

sections.title: Privacy Rules
sections.content:
Measurement data can be as privacy sensitive as location information (RFC 6280), because it is effectively equivalent to location when the context needed to convert it is easy to get. It MUST be protected as well as location information. Over HELD, the confidentiality and authentication of TLS MUST be used, and other protocols MUST provide comparable guarantees.

The model is simple. The Device alone may distribute measurement data, and it MUST do so only as explicitly authorized by a Rule Maker. No entity may redistribute it. A LIS MUST NOT reveal measurement data to any other entity, and MUST NOT reveal location based on it unless the Device directs it to. By including data in a request, the Device implicitly allows the LIS to produce the requested location, and nothing more.

A LIS MUST discard measurement data after servicing a request unless the Device grants permission otherwise. A Device that requests a location URI allows the LIS to use the data for later requests to that URI, but not past the expires time, and the LIS MUST NOT retain data at all if expires is absent. A third party (see RFC 6155) may supply measurement data only if authorized, and the LIS must either trust it for that type of data or validate the data first.
sections.eli5: Your clues about where you are are private, almost like your address. The helper may use them for your question only, and must throw them away afterwards unless you say otherwise.

sections.title: Threats and Mitigations
sections.content:
The threat model focuses on a Device supplying falsified, stolen or incorrect data. Named attacks include:

  • Acquiring location without authorization: supplying measurements for a different Device. LLDP data is broadcast on a network segment, so an attacker there can easily get matching data.
  • Extracting or exposing network topology: even random guesses can map a network if attempts are free. A Device MUST NOT provide topology information without a clear signal that the recipient is authorized. A LIS discovered with DHCP (RFC 5986) can be considered authorized.
  • Lying by proxy: falsified data makes the LIS look as if it vouches for a false location. GNSS data is easy to falsify.
  • Replay and environment spoofing: static measurements can be reused, and radio signals can be faked or amplified.

The mitigations are measurement validation (which MUST be used if an unauthorized recipient could easily obtain the Device's data), location validation by comparison with a trusted location, supporting observations such as a sample of the measured radio signal, and attribution through the PIDF-LO source label. A Device MUST authenticate the LIS as described in Section 9 of RFC 5985.
sections.eli5: Someone might lie about the clues, copy old ones, or fake a signal. The helper can double check, compare with what it knows, and mark answers that depend on your word.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC creates a new IANA registry for GNSS types, run under Specification Required with an Expert Reviewer appointed by the IESG. Each entry gives the GNSS name, a brief description, a token, the signal tokens and a documentation reference. Two systems are registered initially: GPS and Galileo.

It also registers a set of URN sub-namespaces and XML schemas, covering the measurement source, the container, the base types, and the LLDP, DHCP, WiFi, cellular, GNSS and DSL schemas. The XML schemas themselves are given in Section 8 of the RFC.
sections.eli5: It keeps an official list of satellite systems and gives each kind of clue its own official name, so everybody uses them the same way.
